text: Least privilege asks does this one account have too much access. Segregation of duties asks a different question: can one person, alone, complete an entire sensitive process end to end. Even if every permission is individually justified, letting one person hold all of them removes the independent check that catches a mistake or stops fraud.

Accounts payable is the textbook case. Who creates a vendor record, who approves it, and who issues payment are three separate functions. If the same person can create a fake vendor, approve it, and pay it, there's no independent check anywhere in that chain, which is exactly how a lot of real-world payment fraud happens. Split those three across three people, and committing fraud now requires collusion, a much higher bar than acting alone.

This maps directly onto the four access-governance roles, requester, approver, provisioner, auditor. If the same person can request their own access and approve it, there's no independent check on that grant, the identical flaw as the vendor example, applied to access instead of money. That's why access governance programs explicitly forbid self-approval, and keep the provisioner separate from the approver wherever practical.

A toxic combination is a specific pair of permissions that should never sit with the same person. Can create a vendor plus can approve payments is one. Can grant database access plus can approve their own access requests is another. Can write to the audit log plus can read it with no independent review is a third, because that lets someone both commit and cover up an action. An SoD conflict matrix lists sensitive functions and flags which pairs are toxic.

Running a person's actual entitlements against that matrix surfaces violations nobody designed on purpose, often the same permission-creep pattern from last lesson. Next up: access reviews and certification, the process that catches exactly this.
